system.name: Melange member psychometrics (Big Five, dispositions, persona)
system.description: Measuring legislator personality and behavioural dispositions from text and behaviour. Covers the lexical Big Five pipeline (Ramey-style, with SMOreg and RKH calibration), the LLM item-level reader, the ridge hybrid, the CT-CM latent model, behavioural dispositions, cooperation_v2, affective N, the agency/communion persona channel, shrinkage rules, and the genre-transfer tests. These feed the receptivity layer.

components.name: Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)
components.computes: Corpus-relative Big Five z (O, C, E, A, ES; N = -ES) from category rates of floor speech and interviews.
components.method: Rates per 1000 words (LIWC-analog, Empath, MATTR, Brysbaert concreteness) are z-scored and combined with linear weights from published correlates or SMOreg (Mairesse) fit on essays, then refit to RKH targets per trait (hybrid). Shrinkage z x sqrt(tokens/1500). Held-out CV vs RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214 (mean .350). O was reversed on the party check.
assumptions: RKH estimates are a valid reference (method-shared, so convergence is inflated)
Scores are meaningful only within this corpus
empirical_questions: Do text-derived traits converge with expert or insider ratings of the same legislators (Personality on the Hill)?
Is convergence with RKH inflated by shared method (Mairesse-LIWC on both sides)?
Do traits generalize across genres (floor vs interview vs social)?
components.heading: Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)

components.name: Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria
components.computes: Pass or miss of trait validity looks. E and A pass both panels; O passes academics only; N passes insiders only; C has an insider association only.
components.method: Pre-registered looks: interview C vs votes cast rho +0.155 PASS; C vs follow-through +0.112 PASS. Several improvement rounds MISSed. A-ES about .44 is population-real (RKH benchmark) plus about .21 text-tone halo. Status labels must accompany any external claim.
empirical_questions: Does text-measured conscientiousness predict roll-call participation and bill follow-through out of sample?
Is the A-ES correlation in text a halo artifact or a population feature?
components.heading: Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria

components.name: LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model
components.computes: De-identified, chunked LLM ratings on 20 items; ridge hybrid on lexical, interaction and persona features; CT-CM SEM with an LLM method factor.
components.method: The LLM reader removes names before scoring and codes 'cannot tell' as 0. It is display-only. Pink x behavioural diagonal mean +0.064 < 0.12 fails. CT-CM is a one-look capstone.
assumptions: Judge halo is a single method factor
empirical_questions: Do de-identified LLM trait ratings converge with gold panels above lexical methods?
How much of the LLM trait variance is a single halo factor?
components.heading: LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model

components.name: Behavioural dispositions
components.computes: Cooperation, diligence (roll-call participation, LEP), dominance (turn statistics, leadership), visibility (interviews), breadth (portfolio) and reactivity (interview cutoff).
components.method: z-score composites with coverage floors; missing values are neutral.
assumptions: Turn-share statistics index dominance (Rienks & Heylen; Valente)
empirical_questions: Do behavioural dispositions predict lobbying responsiveness better than text traits (prospective H1/H2)?
components.heading: Behavioural dispositions

components.name: Cooperation v2 (share-based bridging)
components.computes: Mean of within-chamber z of cross-party tie share and directional cross-party cosponsorship share (at least 10 cosponsorships). Reciprocity is reported only.
components.method: Volume-free by design. Promoted 2026-07-10. Correlates rho .888 with bpf.
assumptions: Cross-party share measures cooperation independent of volume
empirical_questions: Is cross-party cosponsorship share stable across Congresses (trait-like)?
components.heading: Cooperation v2 (share-based bridging)

components.name: Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests
components.computes: affective_n = z(LIWC i + negemo - posemo) + z(LLM pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility), residualized on E and party.
components.method: Gate 5/5 passed: |r(N,E)| .039; party .000; LIWC-LLM convergence +.236; split-half SB .742. Promoted 2026-07-11. Genre transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text FAILED (rho .050, .161).
assumptions: Negative-emotion and first-person-singular words track N (Pennebaker)
No gold N criterion exists, so the gate tests construct integrity only
empirical_questions: Does interview-derived affective N transfer to other speech genres?
Does affective N predict yielding under pressure (Byrne mechanism) in observed behaviour?
components.heading: Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests

components.name: Agency/communion persona channel
components.computes: persona_z = 0.60 z(communion) - 0.40 z(agency) from LLM few-shot cue classification (strong 1.0, weak 0.5), blended at PERSONA_W 0.30.
components.method: Functional gate 18/18. Party signature: communion D .099 vs R .049. Persona homophily is not earned (|r| <= 0.015).
assumptions: Projected persona is what a lobbyist meets
empirical_questions: Do communal-persona members accept more meetings or cosponsor more with outside requesters?
components.heading: Agency-communion persona channel

components.name: Interview weighting (C_INT_W) and gated shrinkage (P6)
components.computes: Conscientiousness aggregates interview chunks at 2x. Members with fewer than 8 measurements are shrunk.
components.method: The P6 reliability claim (.748 -> .831) was retracted as double-shrink inflation; the change was kept on external criterion gains.
assumptions: Shrinkage is judged only on external criteria, not split-half reliability
empirical_questions: Does shrinkage of thin-corpus members improve correlation with external criteria?
components.heading: Interview weighting (C_INT_W) and gated shrinkage (P6)

positions.paul_position: Paul calls Ramey 'dated but foundational' and asks for frameworks specific to each venue. Birkenmaier's highlights criticize Ramey's SVM as outdated and unvalidated, which is the tension the system's RKH calibration inherits.
Paul highlighted Birkenmaier's validation framework (codebook, Krippendorff alpha 0.70 to 0.78, macro-F1 below 0.80). His notes do not reflect the system's single-look MISS record.
Paul endorses LLM-based trait reading: GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 were the only models validated.
Indirect support: effort allocation is observable, and conscientiousness relates to sponsorship.
This is the most direct transfer from Paul's notes: pre-built codebooks and node design. His weaknesses are the conversion from trait to node and ambiguous statements.

evidence.title: How Do Electoral Incentives Affect Legislator Behavior? Evidence from U.S. State Legislatures
evidence.claim: Floor-vote participation is state-dependent within the same legislator. It falls 2.70 points (SE 0.53) from a mean of 90.48 in the final term, about a 27% proportional rise in abstention. Committee activity falls about 8% (-0.31 from 3.84).
evidence.system_side: diligence_z is the mean of z-log votes_cast within chamber (with a full-term guard at 25% of the chamber median) and LEP follow-through. It is labelled a C-role disposition and enters susceptibility at -0.20. Members on the retiring list therefore get lower diligence and higher susc, which partly offsets their incent 0.60. Electoral status enters the pressure term twice, with opposite signs, and is never modelled explicitly.
evidence.transfer: Moderate. Missing votes is a universal congressional behaviour, and the paper's within-person identification is cleaner than anything the system has. However, the state final-term drop of about 3 points is small next to the cross-member spread in congressional votes_cast. It matters most for members in their final Congress, or those campaigning for another office, whose absences are campaign-driven. The disposition reading holds only after electoral status is held fixed.

evidence.title: How Do Electoral Incentives Affect Legislator Behavior? Evidence from U.S. State Legislatures
evidence.claim: Roll-call participation moves with electoral incentives inside the same person (-2.70 points in the final term, mean 90.48). As a criterion it therefore mixes trait and electoral situation.
evidence.system_side: The interview-genre C criterion is a Spearman correlation between C and votes_cast (recorded PASS, rho +0.155), computed cross-sectionally with no stratum for electoral status (retiring or running for other office).
evidence.transfer: Weak to moderate. The PASS is recorded and must not be re-run (single-look). The paper shows the criterion has a situational component, so any external claim from this look should carry an UNSTRATIFIED label on electoral status. This matters most if campaign-driven absences correlate with interview volume, for example among members running statewide.

evidence.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress: A Political Economic History of Roll Call Voting
evidence.claim: Average between-party and within-party pairwise distances (Figs 7-8, 1879-1998) show polarization declining to WWII, stable until the late 1970s, and rising steadily since. The paper does not state that the most extreme members sit farthest from the opposing party; that is an analyst inference.
evidence.system_side: dw_control.py docstring records cooperation_v2_z vs |dim1| = -0.250 (n = 532/533, 2026-07-10) and states the extremity control is essential for A.
evidence.transfer: The paper supplies context for why an extremity control matters in a polarized chamber; it does not test the cooperation measure.

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: Few-shot prompting with a codebook of strong and weak agency and communion cues, positive poles only, reaches macro-F1 0.77 (DeepSeek-V3) and 0.76 (GPT-4o) on strong-balanced human labels, the two top configurations. The paper says only these two models pass the functional test units, on strong labels.
evidence.system_side: agency_communion_llm.py ports the codebook and the positive-pole rule (lines 56-60), weights strong cues 1.0 and weak 0.5 (line 232), and runs an 18-unit self-test (lines 99-121: 3 agency, 3 communion, 6 opposite-pole, 6 unrelated) with a pass bar of 16 of 18 (line 121). Default model is claude-sonnet-5 (line 24).
evidence.transfer: The paper's macro-F1 figures belong to GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 on German sentences scored against three trained coders. The system has no human-labelled sentence test, so its macro-F1 is unknown. The 18 units were written by the builder in English; the paper's Appendix J was not available. Only the design and the functional gate transfer.

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: Models told to detect only strong cues perform better than strong-plus-weak definitions, as expected. Table 2 gives DeepSeek-V3 few-shot balanced 0.77 (strong, SD 0.02) against 0.76 (weak plus strong, SD 0.01). No delta is reported.
evidence.system_side: sentences_for keeps every self-referential sentence and weights weak cues 0.5 (lines 124-151, 232). The cache stores the strength label (line 219), but no strong-only score is computed. agency_raw and communion_raw count labels without the weighting, so they are not strong-only scores.
evidence.transfer: The 0.01 gap sits inside the reported SDs and is a single configuration, so the paper supports a direction, not a magnitude. A strong-only score could be computed from the existing cache at no API cost to test whether member ordering changes.

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: Party-level communion share falls from left to right on CHES: LINKE 19 percent, Greens 12, SPD 10, CDU 8, AfD and FDP about 6. The paper shows regression lines and standard-error bars but gives no coefficients, N or intervals in the main text.
evidence.system_side: The brain note records a party signature of D .099 against R .049 for the Claude instrument, and says the top communion members are progressive Democrats. These figures were not recomputed from data in this check.
evidence.transfer: Six German parties against a two-party US Congress, with sentence-level shares against member-level scores. The paper gives no pooled coefficient to compare magnitudes. The gap supports convergent validity but also means the persona score carries party, so any pooled use is UNSTRATIFIED across D and R.

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: Three coders (the first author and two RAs) reached Krippendorff alpha of .70 to .78 for agency and communion, and .72 to .73 for detecting any cue. The paper calls this acceptable and sufficient in Sec 3.2.1.3 and 4.1 and moderate in Sec 5. No computational model exceeded macro-F1 0.80.
evidence.system_side: The 2026-07-04 brain ruling, as cited by the rel, says the paper's coders reached only alpha about .72 on an easier ternary task, and uses that to set aside the single-rater gold test (agency rho +0.035, communion -0.245, n=30). Not recomputed here.
evidence.transfer: The paper's alpha is a multilabel agreement measure on sentence cue labels, from three trained coders with a codebook. The single-rater test used 1-9 holistic member ratings. The paper does not call its task easier, and .72 is the presence-detection alpha rather than the agency or communion alpha.

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: Ramey et al. used a pretrained Mairesse SVR, which the paper says lacks validation against human-annotated data and appears outdated. The paper's own bag-of-words SVM, modelled on Ramey's approach, scores 0.55 to 0.63 macro-F1 on its cue task and often fails to reach 50 percent of functional test units.
evidence.system_side: The big5_traits.py header says the Mairesse SMOreg model file is licence-bound, so the build uses published standardized correlates as linear weights, linear instead of SVR (lines 13-16). The brain says the active weights were later refit to RKH and saved as mairesse_smoreg.json; the mean held-out r of 0.350 is brain-sourced.
evidence.transfer: The SVM numbers are the authors' own cue-classification results, not member-level trait regression, so they do not measure this component's accuracy. The critique bites harder because RKH, the reference standard, is itself built on Mairesse-type SVR (paper Sec 2.5 p.5 on Ramey et al.).

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: LLM prompting with a codebook and few-shot examples classifies defined sentence-level cues. Most sentences carry no cue: 94 percent 'none' for strong cues and 89 percent for weak plus strong.
evidence.system_side: big5_llm.py asks 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items, 4 per trait, at item level with 3-point responses. 'Cannot tell' maps to 0 because cues are absent in about 90 percent of political sentences (header lines 3-10). The header explicitly rejects holistic trait rating. The +0.064 diagonal and the 0.12 bar are brain-sourced; 0.064 was found in the brain, but 0.12 was not located.
evidence.transfer: The paper validates a narrow codebook cue task, not item-level Big Five ratings, so its success does not transfer to the Pink reader. Treating cannot-tell as 0 matches the paper's base rate, but it is the builder's design choice.

evidence.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
evidence.claim: SMOreg on standardized LIWC and MRCPD features per member-year; scores relative to the Congressional Record (fn 10); 100 sentence-level bootstraps per member-year; CI width about 0.3 or less above about 5,000 words a year (median member about 11,000 words); optional jackknife over other years.
evidence.system_side: big5_traits.py follows the steps: corpus-standardized features and z-scores relative to this corpus (about lines 236-251); default speech sources CREC and INTERVIEW (lines 36-40); lowconf below LOWCONF_TOKENS=1500 (lines 28, 251); N = -ES (line 22). The docstring (lines 13-16) also says the license-bound SMOreg file is replaced by published-correlate linear weights, a fourth deviation the analyst omitted. The RKH refit exists in fit_smoreg_rkh.py (5-fold held-out r), but no stored output with the .350 figure was found.
evidence.transfer: Transfers as a procedure only. The paper's precision band assumes about 11,000 words per member-year; the 1,500-token floor is far below the paper's 5,000-word band, so the precision claim does not transfer. Refitting to RKH makes RKH convergence a fit statistic, not validation.

evidence.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
evidence.claim: The 2016 paper's only Conscientiousness outcome is the ceremonial-bill share (Table 3). It has no roll-call participation analysis; roll calls appear only in passing as a source of ideal points (p.5).
evidence.system_side: behavioral_dispositions.py docstring (lines 13-14) calls diligence_z, which is roll-call participation, RKH's strongest C criterion. diligence_z is now the mean of participation and LEP follow-through (lines 49-71).
evidence.transfer: The 2016 text does not support the attribution. Whether another RKH work (the 2015 manuscripts cited at pp.15 and 19) uses participation cannot be checked from this text. Treat as a citation fix, not a modelling finding.

evidence.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
evidence.claim: The paper has no direct validation against ground-truth personality measures for legislators. Its validity rests on ideology correlations (Table 1 Model 1, R2 0.10, N 844), LIWC face validity, NPAT response and bill shares. For NPAT, Emotional Stability moves predicted response from about 30 to about 53 percent between -2 and +2 SD (Table 2 Model 4, N 598). The paper says this suggests selection bias; it does not show it.
evidence.system_side: The analyst's description of Senate expert and insider panels, pre-registered single looks and the E/A/O/N/C pattern could not be verified. Brain topic lines 25-32 cite RKH results, not panels. The cited code path is wrong; the file is at fec/members/big5_improvements_eval.py and contains no panel code found by grep.
evidence.transfer: Senate panels against a House paper is a cross-chamber assumption. The paper's NPAT argument concerns self-report surveys, not expert ratings, so it does not directly apply to the panels.

evidence.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
evidence.claim: Emotional Stability's link to anxiety words is somewhat weaker than those for Openness, Conscientiousness and Extraversion (p.11). Agreeableness is also described as weaker (p.11). ES predicts survey response (Table 2) and loads 0.20 (p<0.01) on Common Space in Table 1 Model 1.
evidence.system_side: N = -ES is carried over (big5_traits.py:22). Affective N is E-residualized and party-controlled (emit_affective_n.py:39-59). Brain topic record 6 reports raw r -0.11 (E-cleaned -0.04, not significant) against RKH-ES at n 147, and broad text-N -0.22. The interview-to-floor rho values (.050, .161) were not checked.
evidence.transfer: The paper's weak ES-anxiety link is a face-validity remark, not a ranking of ES as weakest. Party-residualizing may remove ES signal that the paper's ideology check carries.

evidence.title: Evaluating voice samples as a potential source of information about personality
evidence.claim: LIWC 2015 features alone explained 3.13 percent of out-of-sample variance in self-reported Big Five (N=614 students, average sample about 92 words). The authors call the estimates conservative because samples were brief, constrained and drawn from students. Text names pronoun as top LIWC feature for C and negate for E; feature-level explanations are called highly speculative.
evidence.system_side: big5_traits.py builds z-scored Big Five from closed-vocabulary LIWC-style and Empath counts using a Ramey-synth linear model with published-correlate weights as default. It swaps in Mairesse SMOreg weights when liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json exists. Members under 1500 tokens get a lowconf flag, and the file says consumers shrink them; the script itself only sets the flag.
evidence.transfer: The paper's 3.13 percent is a self-report criterion in students with about 92 words per sample. It does not validate the system's fixed signed weights, which the paper did not test. Its small-sample caution supports a thin-corpus floor only by analogy, since Melange members have far more text than 92 words.

evidence.title: Evaluating voice samples as a potential source of information about personality
evidence.claim: Neuroticism was predicted better by linguistic than by vocal features (out-of-sample R-squared about 0.15, about 0.56 after disattenuation; Table 3 best-model rows). Table 2 lists LIWC top-5 features for N as function words, anx, Tone, Analytic and negemo; the text names no single top LIWC feature for N, and first-person singular is not in the N top five.
evidence.system_side: emit_affective_n.py builds an E-residualized, party-controlled z-score from LLM affective facets; the LIWC-style index is only the convergent-validity anchor. Genre tests of this affective-N measure failed (rho 0.050 pooled, rho 0.161 hearing-only), per the brain note on the N-genre question.
evidence.transfer: The paper is student self-report with about 92-word samples; the system measure is an LLM affective-facet score on legislator text. The paper supports text over voice for N only in its own sample. Its top N predictors differ from the system anchor terms (i, negemo, posemo), so the paper does not validate the anchor index.

evidence.title: Who chokes under pressure? The Big Five personality traits and decision-making under pressure
evidence.claim: The paper explains N-driven choking by working memory: pressure and anxiety use up working memory, so neurotic people take the immediate reward. The authors measured no anxiety, mood or working-memory capacity and ran no pressure manipulation check. Self-rated importance did not differ by condition (Low M = 4.68, SD 2.42; High M = 5.17, SD 2.14; ns).
evidence.system_side: affective_n fills the N slot that receptivity_layer labels as Byrne's channel (default RECEPT_N = affective at line 74; used at line 179). The bearing also cites the project's H5 test of N x loss domain (partial r = +0.036, n = 441) as a null.
evidence.transfer: Byrne gives a theoretical reason to keep an N slot but no evidence that text-measured affective content captures the anxiety facet the paper invokes. The paper's mechanism was never measured, so a null in legislators neither confirms nor refutes Byrne. The N contribution keeps its UNVERIFIED label (DE-062).

evidence.title: Who chokes under pressure? The Big Five personality traits and decision-making under pressure
evidence.claim: The agreeableness result rests on self-report BFI agreeableness predicting worse task performance. It is exploratory and significant only in the uncontrolled Exp 2 (b = .36, p < .01). The paper has nothing on projected or communal rhetoric.
evidence.system_side: The persona channel reads warm or communal rhetoric as approachable-agreeable and blends persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) minus .40 z(agency) into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30 (line 191).
evidence.transfer: Byrne concerns self-reported trait A and says nothing about communal rhetoric in public statements. Citing Byrne for the persona direction is a second inferential step the paper does not cover. PERSONA_W is owner policy; this note is about provenance only.

evidence.title: The influence of personality traits on the effect of persuasion strategies: A systematic literature review
evidence.claim: Agreeableness is the most susceptible trait, which fits communal rhetoric as a sign of being approachable. Extraversion is above average in susceptibility, with liking and commitment working best, which runs against treating assertive or agentic presentation as resistance.
evidence.system_side: persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) - .40 z(agency), blended into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30. Dominant or assertive rhetoric is treated as resisting pressure.
evidence.transfer: Agency and communion are not Big Five dimensions, and mapping agency onto extraversion is loose. The positive communion sign gets mild support; the negative agency sign gets none. PERSONA_W stays, per the owner's ruling, and this bearing concerns only the signs inside the channel.

evidence.title: Going Global: 39 Language Versions of the BFI-2-XS
evidence.claim: Item rewording is treated as a comparability risk: each change request was coded by MQM type and approved only for major issues, 3 requests were rejected as preferential, and mean item change was 10 percent per version pre-Field-Trial (range 0-80) and 6 percent post (range 0-53, 13 of 39 versions).
evidence.system_side: The LLM reader uses 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items (4 per trait), not BFI-2 items. Any change to item text or keying is a new itemset version and a new cache key. v2 rewrote C1, C2, C4, E4 and S2 after ceiling effects of 86-94 percent on 202 pilot chunks.
evidence.transfer: Holds only as a governance analogy. Translation of self-report items is a different measurement problem from an LLM rater applying observer items to political text. The paper reports no psychometric consequences of its changes, so it cannot calibrate how much rewording matters. The system's itemset versioning already enforces the point.

evidence.title: Going Global: 39 Language Versions of the BFI-2-XS
evidence.claim: The authors argue that a standardized, parallel adaptation makes the 39 versions more likely to be comparable than independent national translations. They report no psychometric evidence for this: multi-group CFA alignment was run on Field Trial data (about 450 to 1,800 respondents per country) but the results are confidential, and the versions are described as not yet fully validated.
evidence.system_side: Every lexical trait z is standardized within the current speech corpus, so scores are comparable only inside that corpus. Genre transfer of interview-derived affective N to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050 and .161), per the component record.
evidence.transfer: The analogy maps languages and countries onto speech genres (interview, floor, hearing, social). It supports demanding empirical invariance evidence before pooling or comparing scores across genres, rather than relying on a uniform procedure. It provides no method or numbers the system could import.

evidence.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
evidence.claim: Self-reported Big Five correlate with LIWC categories at most |rho| .08-.14 (abstract p. 843). The 52 categories explain a mean R2 of 5.07 percent of self-report variance (narrow categories, k = 25 self-report samples, n = 83,243-84,084). About 87 percent of that n is Schwartz et al. 2013 (n = 72,809). Heterogeneity significant in 96 percent of cue-validity effects. Table 7 lists LIWC best-category average r = .10 (self) against Moreno et al. .27, HTTP .31, IBM-WPI .13 and human judges .12, all uncorrected.
evidence.system_side: Code matches the description. Exemplar lists include swear = damn hell crap (big5_traits.py:100). Per-1000-word rates are at :220. Hand-set weights W are at :179-185, the SMOreg override at :186-189, and corpus z-scoring at :241-242. The stated held-out CV mean .350 and E .510 were not found in the brain topic or the fec tree. The brain topic records only C +0.348 held-out (round 2, 2026-07-08).
evidence.transfer: Paper samples are mostly informal English social media and student or general-population samples, LIWC 2001-2015. Congressional speech is formal and partly staff-written, and the paper shows formality attenuates markers. The system uses exemplar lists, not licensed LIWC dictionaries, so category equivalence is unverified. Table 7 values are post hoc best-category maxima and cannot rank methods.

evidence.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
evidence.claim: Bivariate cue-validity effects (self-report, Table 3): Openness words over six letters rho .11; Conscientiousness negative emotion -.12, swear -.11, anger -.10; Agreeableness anger -.14, swear -.10, negative emotion -.10, positive emotion .10. Emotional Stability has no first-person singular validity effect at |rho| .10 or more. Cue utilization (observer): Emotional Stability first-person singular -.29.
evidence.system_side: Verified SMOreg weights: A anger -.0202 (json line 66), A swear -.0323 (:87), C anger -.0556 (:95), C swear -.0446 (:116), O sixltr +.0292 (:147). The paper agrees on these signs. Disagreements: ES first-person singular +.0094 (:43), ES negative emotion -.0002 (:51), and E positive emotion -.0339 (:20). The rel line citations were wrong for A anger (cited :43).
evidence.transfer: The paper estimates are bivariate correlations. SMOreg weights are multivariate, so suppression can flip signs without error. The ES first-person comparison sets an observer-based paper effect against a model fit to other data, so it is not like-for-like. The flagged signs remain UNVERIFIED (DE-062) and are an audit lead only.

evidence.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
evidence.claim: Observer-rated (cue utilization, k = 5, n = 1,637, mostly zero-acquaintance raters) explained variance averages 38.52 percent against 5.07 percent for self-report cue validity. Largest observer |rho| .39 (Agreeableness swear) and .31 (Extraversion word count). Emotional Stability has the lowest observer R2 at 31.48 percent. The authors say valid or utilized cues are not the same as true personality.
evidence.system_side: Senate panels are 129 insiders and 125 academics (brain topic line 52). The brain topic says E and A clear both panels, and O, C and N are one-panel association supported (line 58). The rel's per-panel splits (O academics only, N insiders only, C insider only) and the A-ES figures of about .44 and .21 halo do not appear in the brain topic. The cited file fec/big5_improvements_eval.py is not in the repo.
evidence.transfer: The paper observer samples are k = 5 with n = 1,637, nearly all zero-acquaintance. The Senate panels are informed insiders and experts, which the paper could not test. SOKA predicts the overt traits (E, A) would pass and ES would be weakest, which fits the brain topic. Panel convergence shows raters and text use the same cues, not trait accuracy.

evidence.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
evidence.claim: Emotional Stability relates negatively to negative-emotion words (cue validity rho -.12, p. 853) and to first-person singular pronouns (cue utilization rho -.29). Emotional Stability carries 6 of the 20 kernel markers (p. 853). The Emotional Stability negative-emotion validity effect weakens with publication year (Table 6, b = .006). No positive-emotion effect for Emotional Stability is reported.
evidence.system_side: The anchor in emit_affective_n.py counts first-person pronouns, a hand-written negative-affect regex and a hand-written positive-affect regex in interview text of 800 or more words, then z-scores them. These are custom lexicons, not LIWC dictionaries, despite the LIWC framing. Since round 7b the anchor is convergent-validity only (r = +.24 per the rel). Genre-transfer values (.050, .161) were not checked here.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports the sign structure for Emotional Stability only, and it reports heterogeneity by mode and formality. An expected anchor size near .24 is the analyst's inference, not a paper result. This is direction support only, not evidence that N predicts yielding.

evidence.title: Twenty Years of Personality Computing: Threats, Challenges and Future Directions
evidence.claim: Text Personality Recognition SotA is an average correlation of about 0.30 over a 0.133 baseline (WASSA2024 Rho 0.300; PANDORA talks 0.292). Among 45 text systems: SVM 20, neural networks 12, Naive Bayes 10; social network data 27, Essays 15; psycho-linguistic features 16 homogeneous, 20 broader.
evidence.system_side: big5_traits.py implements a Ramey-style pipeline: closed-vocabulary category rates z-scored across the corpus, combined with Mairesse SMOreg weights when liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json exists, otherwise published-correlate weights.
evidence.transfer: Paper figures are against self-report in general-user corpora. The system's held-out CV figure against RKH is not a Recognition benchmark and must not be compared with 0.30 as if it were. The CV figure (.350, with E .510 to O .214) was not found anywhere in the Melange fec tree. fit_smoreg_rkh.py produces candidate refit weights promoted only on REFIT WINS, so the summary's claim that weights are refit to RKH should say candidate, not active.

evidence.title: Twenty Years of Personality Computing: Threats, Challenges and Future Directions
evidence.claim: Brunswik lens separates Recognition (self-report target) from Perception (observer-attributed traits). Computer Perception convergent validity is Rho 0.30 against 0.38 for human perception (Hinds and Joinson 2024), with a caveat that settings are not fully comparable. The paper recommends correlation coefficients over median splits.
evidence.system_side: b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py evaluates predictions separately against the senate insider and academic expert panels, reporting continuous per-trait r for each panel.
evidence.transfer: Expert and insider panels are observer judgments, so the Perception figures (0.30 machine, 0.38 human) are the relevant comparison, not the Recognition rows. The paper's figures come from social media, video and smartphone data, not U.S. senators. The claimed pass pattern (E and A pass both panels; O, C, N one each) was not checked against outputs.

evidence.title: Twenty Years of Personality Computing: Threats, Challenges and Future Directions
evidence.claim: Zero-shot GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 infer Big Five from Facebook status updates at average r = 0.29, comparable to specialized ML (Peters and Matz 2024), which is parity rather than superiority. LLM output shows consistent trait profiles (high Agreeableness, high Openness, low Neuroticism), and the paper says these are not psychological states.
evidence.system_side: big5_llm.py uses item-level scoring with 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items, coarse -1/0/+1 responses, cannot-tell coded 0, and de-identification of author name, state, party and title before scoring (deidentify at line 196).
evidence.transfer: The paper's parity result uses users' own casual posts against self-report. The system scores de-identified political text, so a lower figure is expected, and the paper does not support LLM readers beating lexical ones. The Pink x behavioral diagonal (+0.064 against a 0.12 bar, failing) and the display-only status were not checked.

evidence.title: Psychological Aspects of Natural Language Use: Our Words, Our Selves
evidence.claim: Neuroticism goes with more negative-emotion words, fewer positive-emotion words and more first-person singular. Big Five self-report correlations with word use are r = 0.10 to 0.16 in several hundred college students (Pennebaker and King 1999). Depressed students (Rude et al. 2002) used more I, with me, my and mine comparable. Emotion words are under 5 percent of words in speech, writing and poetry.
evidence.system_side: Emitted affective_n in fec/members/emit_affective_n.py is the E-residualized, party-controlled LLM facet score only. The LIWC base (FPS + negemo - posemo) is computed but kept as a convergent anchor (r = +.24 per code comments). The FPS regex pools i, me, my, mine, myself; the paper reports the I-only effect and does not say pooling dilutes it.
evidence.transfer: Paper evidence is student self-reports, student essays and student conversation, not media-trained legislators speaking on the floor or in interviews. The Rude et al. sample is currently versus never depressed students writing personal essays, not a clinical sample as the analyst wrote. Untested for N in politicians.

evidence.title: Psychological Aspects of Natural Language Use: Our Words, Our Selves
evidence.claim: Self-reported Big Five correlates with closed-vocabulary word use at r = 0.10 to 0.16 across several hundred college students with multiple writing samples (Pennebaker and King 1999). Neuroticism goes with negative emotion and I; extraversion with positive emotion and social words; agreeableness with positive and low negative emotion.
evidence.system_side: Hand weights W (big5_traits.py lines 179-185) cite Pennebaker-King, Yarkoni and Mairesse; ES anx -.30, negemo -.25, i -.20 at line 181 confirmed. Dormant when fec/liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json exists (lines 186-189; file present). Reported held-out CV mean .350 (E .510) was not located in fec/members py, md or json files searched; unverified.
evidence.transfer: The paper ceiling applies to text matched to self-report in students. RKH targets are derived from text, so .35 against RKH is not comparable evidence of validity. Hand-weight signs carry over only if the fallback is reactivated. The review does not cite Yarkoni or Mairesse.

evidence.title: Psychological Aspects of Natural Language Use: Our Words, Our Selves
evidence.claim: Word use is consistent across text types for 36 LIWC dimensions (Pennebaker and King 1999). Four-week retest of student everyday conversation (EAR, 52 college students, Mehl and Pennebaker 2002a) was r = 0.41 for standard linguistic variables and 0.24 for psychological-process variables. Successive 2-minute speech intervals correlated 0.51 across 21 categories, a result the review attributes to Gleser et al. 1959 on 5-minute talks.
evidence.system_side: Genre-residualized refit with MTMM bar (b5_residual_eval.py docstring lines 9-10), and the parent family failing it, are stated in the docstring. The interview affective N transfer figures (rho .050, .161) were not located in the cited lines or elsewhere searched. RITUAL stripping exists in big5_traits.py lines 22-24.
evidence.transfer: The paper consistency evidence comes from diaries, college writing assignments, journal abstracts and recorded student conversation, not all self-authored. Floor, press and social text is outside its scope. The inference that 0.24 retest reliability predicts weak genre transfer is the analyst's, not the paper's.

evidence.title: Psychological Aspects of Natural Language Use: Our Words, Our Selves
evidence.claim: In at least two studies (Pennebaker and Francis 1996; Berry et al. 1997), judges' ratings of emotionality correlated more highly with the language of texts and speech than with the writers' or speakers' self-reports. No coefficients are given, and the review raises the gold-standard question.
evidence.system_side: Validity is judged against observer panels and RKH. Halo removal (ct_p2 in big5_improvements_eval.py lines 218-227) and the A-ES and discriminant bars (line 434) exist. The .44 figure is the RKH anchor (.443) used as a reference, not a recorded system A-ES correlation. The .21 text-tone halo attribution was not located.
evidence.transfer: Observer panels rate senators partly from the same public speech the readers score, so convergence can reflect shared observable cues. That halo mechanism is the analyst's inference, not stated in the review. The evidence is two studies in emotion, not Big Five panels.

evidence.title: Predicting the Big 5 personality traits from digital footprints on social media: A meta-analysis
evidence.claim: Pooled random-effects r per trait: O .39 [.30,.48], C .35 [.29,.42], E .40 [.33,.46], A .29 [.21,.36], N .33 [.27,.39], 16 effect sizes each. Heterogeneity I2 93.15-97.46. Each study contributed its best model or highest single-feature effect. Paper-side numbers reproduced exactly from Table 2 (Z, Q, I2, tau2).
evidence.system_side: Code matches the description: closed-vocabulary standardized linear model with corpus z-scoring over member posts plus CREC and INTERVIEW speech (big5_traits.py docstring and source setup). The Birkenmaier citation is in the docstring. NOT FOUND: the held-out CV against RKH (E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214, mean .350). data/members/big5_v2.json holds held-out r against behavioral targets: A .059 (cooperation_z), C .281 (diligence_z), E .563 (visibility_z), O .135 (breadth_z); ES has no held-out r (v1 fallback).
evidence.transfer: Azucar's pooled r is not a benchmark for this system. Its criterion is self-report from lay users; the system's held-out targets are behavioral dispositions, and no RKH held-out figure exists in the repo. Heterogeneity is over 93 percent and best-model selection probably inflates the pooled values. Any citation must carry the label UNSTRATIFIED (16 studies, 4 platforms, 2012-2017; two included studies, Farnadi 2016 Study 1 and Kosinski 2013, used MyPersonality data). The ordering claim as first written is wrong: in Azucar E (.40) is highest and O (.39) second; A (.29) is lowest. In this system O is the weakest trait on the breadth target (.135), which is not an inversion of a best-predicted trait.

evidence.title: Predicting the Big 5 personality traits from digital footprints on social media: A meta-analysis
evidence.claim: Demographics (age, gender) as a moderator raised accuracy for N (beta .25, p<.05, R2 .19) and A (beta .25, R2 .19). O showed a marginal gain (beta .26, R2 .12, p=.09).
evidence.system_side: affective_n is the LLM affective facets residualized on E, then on party, then z-scored (emit_affective_n.py lines 52-56). The gate comment at line 43 reads party .00. The residualization controls for party and E only; age and gender are not controlled in these lines.
evidence.transfer: The paper's demographic moderator is between-study and univariate: whether a study used demographic features, with no adjustment. It does not show an individual-level mechanism. The paper says its demographic finding is consistent with survey literature on demographic differences in self-reported traits (Goldberg 1998; Soto 2011). The analyst's claim that the gain comes from group membership correlating with self-reported traits, a predictive shortcut, goes beyond the paper. Do not adopt demographic predictors on the strength of this paper.

evidence.title: Predicting the Big 5 personality traits from digital footprints on social media: A meta-analysis
evidence.claim: Social-media activity statistics (posts, friends, network density, likes received, comments, tags) gave a marginal increase in E accuracy (beta .19, R2 .18, p=.06). The paper reports no other significant moderator effects; it does not report a tested null for each trait.
evidence.system_side: visibility_z is broadcast engagement: log counts of attributed interviews and interview programs, for members with at least 3 interviews (behavioral_dispositions.py line 18; visibility block near lines 111-113). Dominance uses floor turn statistics plus committee leadership. The visibility measure is press-interview engagement, not social-media activity.
evidence.transfer: The constructs differ. The paper's activity variables are social-media posting, friend counts and network density; the system's variable counts press or broadcast interviews. Any link is an analogy, not support, and it bears on E only, not on the lexical E it was meant to contrast with. The analyst's point that interview counts track press-office scheduling and seniority is their inference and was not checked against the repo.

evidence.title: Predicting the Big 5 personality traits from digital footprints on social media: A meta-analysis
evidence.claim: Combining several footprint types gave significant gains for O (beta .27, R2 .16), C (beta .25, R2 .20) and N (beta .21, R2 .14). E showed a trend (beta .18, R2 .12, p=.08). A showed no gain. Text or pictures alone added nothing over other types.
evidence.system_side: The v3 hybrid ridge combines lexical features, 8 interaction-channel features and agency/communion persona cues, with nested 5-fold CV and honest held-out r (big5_hybrid.py docstring lines 3-12; heldout_r lines 46-62). The committed artifact data/members/big5_v3_hybrid.json shows no gain over lexical-only: A hybrid .056 vs lexonly .059; C .273 vs .281; E .564 vs .563; O .130 vs .135. The hybrid docstring says interaction features are nickname-degraded until re-ingest, so these numbers are a floor.
evidence.transfer: The paper concerns social-media footprint types measured against self-report among lay users. The hybrid adds interaction-channel features that are not footprint types, and its targets are behavioral. The paper gives no basis for expecting a gain from interaction features. In the system's own output the added features gave no held-out gain on any target, so the paper does not support the current hybrid. Any future claim needs a pre-registered look and second-path reproduction (DE-062).

evidence.title: The Effect of Politicians' Personality on Their Media Visibility
evidence.claim: Extraversion is positive and significant in the pooled OLS: b = 0.129 (SE 0.052), beta .117, p < .05 (Model 1, n = 306, R2 = .483, country dummies and controls). Also significant on news websites (Model 3, b = 0.117, p < .05).
evidence.system_side: visibility_z in fec/members/behavioral_dispositions.py is the mean of within-chamber z-scores of log interview count and log interview-program count, computed only for members with at least 3 interviews (others neutral). Documented as the extraversion-sociability role. Committee and leadership sit in dominance_z.
evidence.transfer: The extraversion direction holds in the paper, but the effect is small (beta .117). The paper's outcome is earned mentions by journalists, not interviews a member gives. The sample is MPs in Belgium, Canada and Israel, 2011-2015, with self-reported TIPI. Office is the dominant predictor there, so a US interview count needs office controls before it reads as temperament. Any claim that visibility_z double-counts dominance_z is an untested inference, not a paper finding.

evidence.title: The Effect of Politicians' Personality on Their Media Visibility
evidence.claim: Net of office, activity, Facebook output and controls, MPs who are more neurotic (beta -.111) and more agreeable (beta -.116) appear less in national news (Table 1 Model 1). The authors attribute this to temperament, not to interview selection, which they do not test.
evidence.system_side: affective_n is the default N-slot (RECEPT_N defaults to affective, receptivity_layer.py:74; read at lines 83-89). Its base is LIWC counts from the interview corpus plus LLM affective facets, party-controlled (fec/members/emit_affective_n.py lines 2-7). Members without a row get neutral 0 (receptivity_layer.py:179). visibility_z sets members with fewer than 3 interviews to neutral (behavioral_dispositions.py:111-114).
evidence.transfer: The paper finds airtime selects on temperament among MPs, which would make interview-derived N range-restricted. Whether US interview coverage selects this way is untested. The paper concerns earned news coverage, not interviews a member gives. Test: correlate interview coverage with non-text proxies such as reactivity_z after chamber-leadership controls. The affective N is also residualized on text-E and party, which the paper does not discuss.

evidence.title: The Effect of Politicians' Personality on Their Media Visibility
evidence.claim: Extraversion appears in observable media presence (beta .117 pooled; b = 0.117, p < .05 on websites; p < .1 for newspapers and TV). TIPI Cronbach alphas are .75 extraversion, .39 openness, .53 neuroticism, .40 conscientiousness and .15 agreeableness. The agreeableness item pair correlates r = .09, p > .1.
evidence.system_side: The receptivity layer comment reads lexical E as broadcast talkativeness and replaces it with behavioral dispositions (receptivity_layer.py:59-60). The lexical Big Five in big5_traits.py is scored by default from social posts, floor speech (CREC) and INTERVIEW text (lines 30-40), and lowconf traits are shrunk by token count with LOWCONF_TOKENS defaulting to 1500 (lines 20 and 28).
evidence.transfer: The paper does not say an E-broadcast-volume link is partly expected for real extraverts. It says extraversion reflects need for interaction and public recognition (lines 884-887). Overlap between text-E and interview volume is possible but not shown. Lexical E also draws on posts and floor speech, so the circularity point applies only in part. The paper calls the TIPI sufficiently valid overall (line 538), so the claim that elite self-report is not usable for A, O or C is the analyst's inference.

evidence.title: How to train your stochastic parrot: large language models for political texts
evidence.claim: Few-shot LLM classification can match or beat crowd and expert coding, but results depend heavily on prompt design and need checks against hand labels the prompt was not tuned on.
evidence.system_side: agency_communion_llm.py uses a few-shot codebook with strong (1.0) and weak (0.5) cue conditions (docstring lines 5-7; method string near lines 238-239) and classifies sentence-level cues. The 18/18 functional gate, the party signature, and the absence of held-out human-gold accuracy were not verified. PERSONA_W was not found in agency_communion_llm.py, so its definition lives elsewhere.
evidence.transfer: The paper validates document-level measures against expert and crowd codes; the cues here are sentence-level and aggregated per member. A paper-style check would need a hand-coded cue sample that was not used to write the codebook. PERSONA_W 0.30 is an owner ruling and is not changed by this review.

evidence.title: Emerging Late Adolescent Friendship Networks and Big Five Personality Traits: A Social Network Approach
evidence.claim: Trait similarity is the strongest selection effect: openness 1.45, extraversion 1.46, agreeableness 1.55 (all p<.001), against ego and alter effects of .01 to .14. It is estimated jointly with outdegree, reciprocity, transitivity, distance-2 and sex, and it varies by group: significant in 7/10, 8/10 and 10/10 groups. Overall profile similarity was not modelled here; the authors' 2009 paper on the same sample found it did not predict friendship intensity.
evidence.system_side: The persona-homophily gate correlates persona compatibility (sum of agency and communion differences, IPC complementarity, communion match only, both warm) with static cosponsor tie weights, with the party confound removed. All four models gave |r| <= 0.015, so the homophily edge weighting stays off.
evidence.transfer: Transfer is weak. The paper's similarity effect appears while self-rated strangers choose friends in the first months, with network structure held fixed. Cosponsorship among sitting legislators is an established, party- and committee-driven tie, not a choice among strangers. The paper does not overturn the null and is no reason to re-propose homophily edge weighting. Its one transferable point: a cross-sectional correlation with no reciprocity or closure controls, using a combined two-trait distance, is a different test from trait-specific similarity estimated inside a selection model. The null therefore holds for the test that was run, not for homophily in general. Any SIENA rerun would be new analysis and would stay UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

evidence.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
evidence.claim: PoliPers defines 15 facets. Table 1 maps Assertiveness & Will to take control to AG: Assertiveness and Empathy & Compassion to COM: Warmth, and gives each facet a named opposite pole (Empathy's is Apathy & Indifference).
evidence.system_side: The persona codebook in agency_communion_llm.py uses the PoliPers names for its two cue classes and scores only the positive poles. The codebook names Birkenmaier & Lechner 2025 as its source. PoliPers does not cite that paper (it cites Repke, Birkenmaier & Lechner 2024, a survey-guide reference), so the link runs through shared authorship, not through PoliPers' citations.
evidence.transfer: The facet definitions transfer as construct definitions. The psychometric evidence does not: it comes from German survey ratings of traits, not from LLM coding of English congressional sentences.

evidence.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
evidence.claim: The Assertiveness facet is not unidimensional. In ideal-politician ratings (Study 3, N=589) it gave two factors because the 'power-hungry, claims leadership' item loaded reversed, and its alpha was not computed (Table A4). In observer ratings of Trump and Merkel (pooled, Study 4, N=211) its alpha was .40 and omega .48 (Table A7). In ideal ratings Assertiveness was the only facet that differed by politician gender (d=.19, p=.025).
evidence.system_side: The self-test treats 'I claim leadership and I am not afraid to use power to get results' as a gold agency unit. The sentence-level agency share pools all agency-labelled sentences, including power-claiming ones, into one score.
evidence.transfer: The split was measured in citizen ratings of traits, not in congressional sentences. Whether power-claiming and leadership-taking cues split in text is untested, so this is a plausibility warning, not a measured defect.

evidence.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
evidence.claim: Observer trait ratings track the rater's ideological proximity (r=.36-.48 on Integrity, Intellect and Creativity) and global evaluation (facet-likeability r up to .76). The authors read this as raters being less objective depending on where they stand politically, and separate positivity from descriptive normativity.
evidence.system_side: The LLM reader removes names, titles and party before scoring (deidentify), and the CT-CM model adds an LLM method factor to absorb judge halo.
evidence.transfer: The paper establishes the human-rater analogue only. That the same bias holds for an LLM's reputational priors is an inference. The CT-CM outcome is a separate matter and is not supported by this paper.

evidence.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
evidence.claim: Observer trait ratings of politicians carry rater-ideology bias (proximity r up to .48). Several 4-item facets have low self-rating reliability (alpha .44-.52: Compromise .51, Humility .46, Loyalty .44, Creativity .45), which limits attainable convergent correlations.
evidence.system_side: Senate insider and academic expert panels are treated as independent gold criteria, and a halo PC1 bifactor removal (P2) was tested against the criteria.
evidence.transfer: PoliPers raters were crowdworkers rating two prominent leaders, not experts rating senators, so the bias evidence is a reason to check panel ratings for partisanship, not proof that they are biased. The limit on convergent correlations is the analyst's inference from reliability.

evidence.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
evidence.claim: Global Big Five domains lack political specificity, and contextualized measures outperform non-contextualized ones. Facets diverge within a domain: Compromise with Agreeableness r=.33 versus Trust r=.50, and Intellect with Emotional Stability r=.41, which the authors call unexpected.
evidence.system_side: Five domain-level z scores are built from closed-vocabulary category rates with linear correlate weights, z-scored within the corpus.
evidence.transfer: The argument concerns survey item design, not text features. A facet-level text reader would need its own validation, and this paper does not change the domain-level validity record.

evidence.title: Online Appendix: Personality on the Hill: Expert Evaluations of U.S. Senators' Psychological Traits
evidence.claim: Table A1 gives Senate-insider and APSA-Fellow mean Big Five ratings for 129 senators, feeding main-paper Tables 2-5. Table A2 gives academic ratings for 126 senator name entries (text count), used only in main-paper Table 1. Each row carries a rating count. Observed values run 1.00-7.00 with 0.50 increments noted by the authors.
evidence.system_side: build_big5_senate_gold.py writes a SHA-256-pinned frozen artifact (data/stance/big5_senate_expert_gold.json) keeping panel, source name, page and ratings_n. EXPECTED_COUNTS is 129 insiders and 125 academics (line 20); the 1-7 range check is at line 62. The artifact has 129 insider and 125 academic records. The academic count is one short of the 126 text entries: the academic Feingold row (malformed cell 4..33, text line 1297) is absent; Feingold appears only as an insider with ratings_n 2. The except branch at lines 56-61 drops that row silently, and its comment that only headings reach it is wrong. The usage contract at lines 85-90 is as stated. Both validators score per panel via map_gold.
evidence.transfer: Senate-only and historic; era unstated. Validates rank order on overlap with current members only, as the code caveat at b5_external_gold_validate.py:209 says. Ratings are as coded by the raters, not self-report.

evidence.title: Online Appendix: Personality on the Hill: Expert Evaluations of U.S. Senators' Psychological Traits
evidence.claim: Senators rated by only one coder are excluded from all analyses in the main paper but still appear in both tables. Bold and italic top and bottom designations apply only to senators with at least two coders.
evidence.system_side: The primary validators do not filter on ratings_n. averaged_gold (b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py:83-97) averages insider and academic values with no count weight. oof_variant (126-134) keeps any row with a non-null trait. row_correlations (b5_external_gold_validate.py:114-118) filters only on null traits. Side probes respect the rule: b5_gold_criterion_probes.py:58-68 stratifies insider k=1 vs k>=2, and b5_o_weighted_look.py:399 weights by sqrt(ratings_n) with a k>=2 subset at line 417.
evidence.transfer: Same data and same inclusion rule. The size of the effect depends on how many current-roster matches are k=1 insiders, which was not counted here. Any k>=2 re-run is a new look under single-look discipline, not a free re-score.

evidence.title: Online Appendix: Personality on the Hill: Expert Evaluations of U.S. Senators' Psychological Traits
evidence.claim: The extremes of both panels are party-skewed. Democrats are 62% of the insider highest scorers and 65% of the lowest (main-paper Table 3, as cited). In the academic table 80% of high scores go to Democrats (Angus King counted as Democrat) and 80% of low scores to Republicans. The note calls the academic table A3; it is labelled A2.
evidence.system_side: The panel pass/miss pattern matches the artifact big5_gold_anchored.json: E and A pass both panels; O passes academics only (insider one-sided permutation p 0.104); N passes insiders only (academic p 0.195). Neither primary validator controls for party: b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py and b5_external_gold_validate.py contain no party term. The ONC look partials out female and republican covariates (b5_onc_dual_panel_look.py:121-164, covariates at 151-153, loader at 188). The claim that lexical O was reversed on a party check is not supported: the ONC candidate file marks O NOT_LOOKED_CRITERION_STOP_BAR_MISS, and no such result was found in the brain notes.
evidence.transfer: Party is a known fault line here. Panel-level correlations should be quoted with party strata or an UNSTRATIFIED label. The suggestion that O passes only against academics because of party is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The 62/65 and 80/80 figures describe only the extremes.

evidence.title: Online Appendix: Personality on the Hill: Expert Evaluations of U.S. Senators' Psychological Traits
evidence.claim: Insider, APSA Fellow and academic raters supply Big Five ratings of senators' public persona, usable as an external criterion for text-derived traits. The appendix calls these Big Five measures built from insider and academic data. It does not call them independent or observer ratings.
evidence.system_side: The panels serve as external gold in b5_external_gold_validate.py and b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py. Full-sample gold-fitted weights are emitted after the OOF verdict (b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py:4-7, 136, 165). b5_profile_basis.py loads the gold artifact at line 128 and passes selected_weights into member_basis at lines 36-44, so for shipped composites the panels are no longer untouched; only the OOF figures are clean. The cited code does not refit the lexical instrument to RKH targets. The v2 lexical builder (big5_lexcal_v2.py docstring, lines 3-12) learns weights against behavioral criteria and describes the RKH and Mairesse weights as v1 priors.
evidence.transfer: Applies to senators who overlap the appendix and to text from the same public-persona era. Does not carry to House members or to genres (floor, interview, social) the raters never saw. Ratings describe perceived public persona, not self-report.

evidence.title: The persuasive effects of political microtargeting in the age of generative artificial intelligence
evidence.claim: The ad openness score comes from a language model trained to predict how attractive a text is to readers high in openness (Simchon et al. 2023, ref 13), not who wrote it; prompted ChatGPT rewrites shift that score by Cohen's d = 0.51 and GPT-3 rewrites by only d = 0.07, so the style can be produced on demand.
evidence.system_side: Melange scores author openness from floor speech and interview text with a closed-vocabulary linear map (O weights sixltr .30, insight .25, article .20, i -.15, certain -.10), refit to RKH targets. Held-out CV vs RKH for O is .214, the weakest of the five traits, and O is checked against an expected negative party sign.
evidence.transfer: The paper shows openness-styled text is easy to generate on demand (d = 0.51 with a simple prompt), which supports the worry that legislators' public text reflects staff and communications strategy rather than author trait; it does not validate author-side lexical O in either direction. Applies to Melange only as a construct-validity caution for O on prepared speech.

evidence.title: Corpus-Based Dictionaries for Sentiment Analysis of Specialized Vocabularies
evidence.claim: LIWC trails the domain-built measure on benchmark accuracy (69.4% vs 80.4% in-sample; 69.7% vs 79.5% held-out). Its unit-level ranks diverge: Burton ranks 1st in the corpus measure and 50th of 84 under LIWC.
evidence.system_side: The live affective N measure is the E-residualized, party-controlled sum of LLM affective facets. The LIWC base was removed as a component (the comment cites Jack Bergman moving from #1 to #412) and kept only as a convergent anchor (r = +.24, gate G3). Verified at emit_affective_n.py comment lines 37-41 and affective_n_validate.py:16-17 and 81-82. The stale component description (z(LIWC) + z(LLM)) was not checked in this pass.
evidence.transfer: The paper measures document polarity in movie reviews and court opinions, not a trait from interview transcripts. Only the general point transfers: closed-vocabulary counts can misfire outside their home register. The paper says nothing about personality or speech.

evidence.title: Machine and deep learning for personality traits detection: a comprehensive survey and open research challenges
evidence.claim: Deep and transformer readers beat TF-IDF/closed-vocabulary shallow ML at trait detection. MBTI experiment: Bi-LSTM + sentence embeddings Ext 92 / Cons 90 / Agr 91 / Open 89; DistilBERT Open 92 / Cons 91; SVM (TF-IDF) Open 89 / Cons 80; POS-DT Cons about 53. The paper reports accuracy only, with no split, cross-validation or variance.
evidence.system_side: The lexical reader works in the style of Ramey et al. It z-scores LIWC-analog, Empath, MATTR and concreteness rates within this corpus and combines them with published-correlate or SMOreg weights, which are then refit to RKH with ridge or LinearSVR. Held-out CV r vs RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214 (mean .350). Members with fewer than 1,500 tokens are flagged lowconf, and consumers shrink them toward 0.
evidence.transfer: Weak transfer. The paper's labels are MBTI types that ordinary social-media users reported about themselves, its unit is the post or user, and its metric is accuracy on dichotomized traits. The system's targets are expert and insider ratings or RKH estimates for about 147 to 533 legislators, scored by held-out correlation. Fine-tuning a deep reader would need thousands of labeled members, and the system has no such set. The paper therefore gives no usable effect size for replacing the lexical reader, and its accuracies must not be compared with the system's r.

evidence.title: Machine and deep learning for personality traits detection: a comprehensive survey and open research challenges
evidence.claim: Text personality datasets lack a direct measure of emotional stability or neuroticism (Sec 1, p.2). The survey's experiment reports only Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness and Openness, with no N/ES result.
evidence.system_side: affective_n combines a Pennebaker LIWC base (first-person singular, negative and positive emotion) with LLM affective facets, controlled for party. Because no gold N criterion exists, its gate tests construct integrity only. Genre transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050, .161).
evidence.transfer: This is a statement about the field, not a test. It confirms that the literature offers no ready-made N criterion the system has missed. It does not validate the system's affective-N construct. It applies regardless of population, because the gap concerns the datasets themselves.

evidence.title: Machine and deep learning for personality traits detection: a comprehensive survey and open research challenges
evidence.claim: LLMs are listed as an open challenge and future direction for personality detection, without an evaluation. BERT and GPT are named most effective in the RQ answers. The paper does not discuss identity leakage, reputational priors or halo.
evidence.system_side: The item-level LLM reader removes author identity (name, state, party, title) before scoring, codes 'cannot tell' as 0, and averages 1,200-word chunks. It is display-only, and its behavioural diagonal mean of +0.064 falls short of the 0.12 bar. The ridge hybrid combines lexical, interaction and persona features under nested CV against behavioural targets.
evidence.transfer: The system's LLM design is already more careful than anything the survey covers (de-identification, observer-keyed items, held-out behavioural criteria). The paper adds no evidence that would move the reader off display-only status.

evidence.title: Learning Personalised Models for Automatic Self-Reported Personality Recognition
evidence.claim: Within the paper's NAS talk-turn models, adding sentiment to duration, content and speech-rate features moves AMSE from 0.874 to 0.942 (generic), 0.883 to 1.074 (age split), and 0.844 to 0.784 (gender split). Single test split, no intervals. The authors themselves expected sentiment to hurt, because their Spanish-only sentiment tool was applied to Catalan and English turns.
evidence.system_side: big5_traits.py builds lexical Big Five from word features with corpus-relative z-scores (lines 17-18), a LOWCONF_TOKENS=1500 flag (line 28), and a party-only external check (around lines 265-275). No sex-stratified check exists in the file.
evidence.transfer: The paper's sentiment features are a Spanish sentiment classifier applied to talk turns, not a lexical trait dictionary, and the paper's own language-mismatch caveat applies. The transferable item is a diagnostic only: report text-trait correlations against the target stratified by sex, or label them UNSTRATIFIED. This paper supports no per-sex models.

evidence.title: Learning Personalised Models for Automatic Self-Reported Personality Recognition
evidence.claim: Among generic single modalities, talk-turn features without sentiment (duration, content, speech rate) average AMSE 0.874 across the five traits, audio 0.920, and FaceBody 1.325 (Table 1, p.65). The paper does not isolate extraversion or dominance and does not test broadcast interviews.
evidence.system_side: behavioral_dispositions.py: dominance_z is the mean of an interaction-channel term (verbal output, floor-holding Gini, floor defense; lines 84-88) and a committee-leadership z (line 89). A header comment cites turn statistics as the replicated dominance signal (line 17).
evidence.transfer: Indirect, five-trait-averaged evidence that turn structure carries trait signal in dyadic lab tasks. It does not validate dominance_z or its committee term, and says nothing about congressional floor speech. Any use should name the window and denominator.

evidence.title: Feasibility of Big Data Analytics to Assess Personality Based on Voice Analysis
evidence.claim: Strongest voice correlates came from zero-acquaintance expert ratings made from video plus audio (E 0.48, N -0.47, C 0.44), not from self-report. The authors read this as judges estimating purely from video and audio evidence. Expert Openness ICC was 0.23 on 20 videos.
evidence.system_side: Brain notes say clean-audio eGeMAPS descriptors feed the de-identified member narrative (brain lines 53 and 63). The code cited, guarded_audio_lines in b5_narratives.py, maps only delivery rate, pitch variation and volume dynamics into descriptive phrases. The persona-channel description (LLM cue classification of text) was not found in the code cited.
evidence.transfer: Loosely supports presenting audio as perceived persona rather than trait. Two raters, 20 ICC videos and an all-female student sample give no validation of any Melange persona weight. PERSONA_W remains an owner ruling and is not tested by this paper.

evidence.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
evidence.claim: PCA of the 60 raw items gave six components (Big Five plus acquiescence) in both samples. Within-person centering removed the sixth. The five centered components had primary loadings averaging .62 (internet) and .61 (student), with congruence .97 or higher. The 15 facet scales gave five components above the scree line (eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32, then 0.56 or lower). Averaging raw unreversed items gives an acquiescence index from 1.00 to 5.00.
evidence.system_side: big5_llm.py docstring line 7 says balanced keying. The ITEMS table has 3 true-keyed and 1 false-keyed item for O, C, E and A (negatives at lines 59, 63, 67, 71) and 2 and 2 for ES (lines 74-75). The keyed mean is at line 344. Under an all-yes response the four 3:1 traits score +0.5 and ES scores 0.
evidence.transfer: The acquiescence mechanism carries over only if the LLM shows a +1 tendency on observer items, which is untested. Under the paper's logic a yea-saying tendency lifts O, C, E and A together and leaves ES alone, so it would not create the A-ES correlation by itself. The paper's content balancing controls acquiescence at the scale level, not at the item level.

evidence.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
evidence.claim: The BFI-2 has 15 facets, three per domain. E: Sociability, Assertiveness, Energy Level. A: Compassion, Respectfulness, Trust. C: Organization, Productiveness, Responsibility. N: Anxiety, Depression, Emotional Volatility. O: Intellectual Curiosity, Creative Imagination, Aesthetic Sensitivity. Domain scales have 12 balanced-keyed items; the 60-item form and scoring key are in the Appendix.
evidence.system_side: b5_panel_items.py holds 15 observer items, three per domain, with REVERSED = E1, A2, C1, C3, N3, O2 (C has two reversed items; E, A, N and O have one each). PROVISIONAL_TEXT is False at line 9, with a note that the wording was verified verbatim against the companion short-form paper. trait_score takes keyed means with no acquiescence correction.
evidence.transfer: This paper does not contain the BFI-2-XS item set. The one-item-per-facet fact and the verbatim check come from the companion short-form paper (Soto and John 2017, JRP), which is not in this item. Three items per domain cannot give facet scores or balanced keying, so the acquiescence results here transfer to the XS panel only weakly. The panel is CANCELED per the memory index, so this bearing is lineage only.

evidence.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
evidence.claim: Self-peer domain agreement ranged .42 to .69 (mean .56) and facet agreement .27 to .73 (mean .49) in the student sample, with 184 peers (60 percent friends, 30 percent romantic partners). Cross-instrument convergence of the BFI-2 with other Big Five measures runs .72 to .92, from NEO PI-R to BFI.
evidence.system_side: fit_smoreg_rkh.py fits SMOreg-type weights to the RKH per-member targets and reports 5-fold held-out Pearson r. The ACTIVE weights are read from liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json (line 56). The docstring carries caveats on persona transfer. The bearing's held-out values (E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214, mean .350) were not found in the script or in fec/liwc.
evidence.transfer: Use the paper's figures only as a rough scale for convergence and self-peer agreement, not as a bar. The paper compares human self-report with human peer report, and its convergence figures come from the student sample. The shared-method claim (Mairesse and LIWC on both sides) is not stated in the script and is not confirmed here.

evidence.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
evidence.claim: Negative Emotionality facets predict different criteria. Peer-rated stress resistance is predicted by Emotional Volatility (r -.47, beta -.32) and Anxiety (r -.46, beta -.28); positive relations by Depression (r -.53, beta -.38). Facets average R2 .33 against .27 for domains across 20 criteria, and BFI-2 facets add significant variance over BFI domains for 14 of 20 criteria. Predictive utility depends more on facet quality than on facet count.
evidence.system_side: emit_affective_n.py line 45 sums the four LLM facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility). Lines 52-56 E-residualize that sum and control for party. Line 42 and line 59 say LIWC is only the convergent-validity anchor and no longer a component, so the affective N is not combined with a LIWC read. The docstring at lines 3-4 still says it combines LIWC and is stale. receptivity_layer.py lines 176-189 feed the N slot into susc_trait at weight .30, and a code comment marks the affective option as the round-7 default.
evidence.transfer: The pressure mechanism fits Anxiety and Volatility more closely than Depression or pessimism. Keeping those components apart is a later measurement question that would need its own prereg and look. Transfer is weak because the paper's criteria are general-population self-report and peer ratings, not legislators' decisions. The genre-transfer rho values and the H5 null were not checked here.

evidence.title: Big Five Personality Predictions From Twitter Using Regression
evidence.claim: Proposes predicting Big Five trait percentages from tweets with TF-IDF, LIWC/psycholinguistic categories, sentiment and profile features, using RF/SVM/NN (Sec 3.3) or NB/SVM/RNN/BERT (Sec 3.5) plus regression. No N, no label source and no accuracy, precision or recall values are reported. It says cross-validation and confusion matrices are used (Sec 3.4) but shows none.
evidence.system_side: A closed-vocabulary LIWC-analog reader (rates per 1000 words, with low-confidence flags below 1,500 tokens), weighted by Mairesse SMOreg and refit to RKH targets. Traits are z-scored relative to this corpus only. Held-out CV against RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214. The system already implements, and has measured, the feature family the paper only proposes.
evidence.transfer: It does not transfer as evidence. There are no labels, no sample, no results, and the genre (general Twitter users) differs from legislators' floor speech and interviews. At most it is a list of candidate features. Its absolute 'percentage' outputs conflict with the system's rule that scores are meaningful only within this corpus. Its accuracy claim stays unverified and should never be cited as a benchmark (DE-062 spirit).

evidence.title: The Role of Emotional Stability in Twitter Conversations
evidence.claim: An unsupervised ES tagger built from Mairesse et al. 2007 linguistic correlations (Table 2) scores 0.625 accuracy against a 0.5 majority baseline on Personage (8 users x 20 sentences). The authors call this in line with the state of the art. Prior text classifiers reached E.Stab. accuracy of 0.531-0.705 (Table 1).
evidence.system_side: big5_traits.py scores ES from closed-vocabulary category rates using Mairesse-lineage weights (ES: anx -.30, negemo -.25, i -.20, negate -.15, posemo +.10) and sets N = -ES. The system's held-out CV against RKH for ES is .258, one of its weakest traits.
evidence.transfer: Shared lineage only: both apply published Mairesse correlates to new text without local supervision. Celli's evidence covers 2011 English tweets from public users and 8 human-rated users. Congressional floor speech and interviews are a different genre and population. The paper does not show that the ES weights transfer, and its accuracy is barely above chance at that sample size. Use it as a historical benchmark for how weak unsupervised ES reading is, never as validation.
