evidence.title: The Role of Emotional Stability in Twitter Conversations
evidence.claim: Validation against Analyzewords (a LIWC-based proxy, worried = neurotic, upbeat = secure) on 18 users: neurotic P 0.8 / R 0.615 / F1 0.695; secure F1 0.462; average F1 0.578. The authors concede the proxy does not measure the Big Five and that upbeat does not equal secure.
evidence.system_side: affective_n is built from E-residualized, party-controlled LLM affective facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility). LIWC (i + negemo - posemo) is kept as the independent convergent-validity anchor (r = +.24, gate G3). No gold N criterion exists.
evidence.transfer: Celli's validation is circular: a LIWC-family feature set scored against a LIWC-family proxy, so agreement partly reflects shared method. The system's LIWC anchor is the same kind of convergence. The paper therefore reinforces the system's own caveat (gate tests construct integrity, not validity) and adds no criterion evidence. It does not carry over as support for N validity.

evidence.title: The Role of Emotional Stability in Twitter Conversations
evidence.claim: Users tend to converse with others who share their emotional-stability trait (trait homophily). This is reported as a frequency pattern in Fig. 4, with no coefficient and no test.
evidence.system_side: Persona homophily was tested on the settled corpus and found UNEARNED (|r| <= 0.015 against an earning bar of |r| >= 0.05). Persona-homophily edge weighting in cosponsor_route.py stays OFF.
evidence.transfer: The trait differs (ES vs agency/communion), and so does the population (2011 Twitter users vs members of Congress). The relation (@-conversation) differs from cosponsorship, and Celli gives no inferential test. The system's measured null on its own data outranks this. Do not cite Celli as grounds to reopen homophily routing.

evidence.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
evidence.claim: On PANDORA DeepPerson reaches AUC 75.0 (+33.7% vs an IBM feature baseline of about 56.1) against best comparator AttRCNN 64.6. The authors say IBM moved away from LIWC toward open-vocabulary GloVe embeddings. In Table 7 the concept encoder adds about 2 pp AUC (68.0 with it vs 66.2 without). The paper does not rank closed-vocabulary scoring as a family.
evidence.system_side: Lexical Big Five in fec/members/big5_traits.py scores each member on closed-vocabulary LIWC/MRC-style per-1000-word category rates, standardizes them across the corpus, and combines them with standardized trait weights (published correlates, or a Mairesse SMOreg-style file when present).
evidence.transfer: The paper's evidence is binary median-split self-report classification on Reddit, Facebook and student essays. The system is judged against RKH and Senate gold panels on congressional speech, which the paper never tests. The held-out CV figure of .350 vs RKH and the refit-to-RKH step were not located in the cited file, so they stay unverified.

evidence.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
evidence.claim: On PANDORA BERT-Base reaches AUC 61.5, RoBERTa 63.2 and PersonaBERT 63.4, against DeepPerson 75.0. DeepPerson was pretrained on 800 million tokens vs 3.3 billion (BERT-Base) and 4.1 billion (PersonaBERT); RoBERTa used about 30 billion or more. The paper's ablation credits pseudo-labeling (SPDFiT) with about a 5-point AUC drop when removed.
evidence.system_side: fec/members/big5_llm.py header: item-level scoring with 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items (4 per trait), coarse -1/0/+1 responses, de-identified chunks of about 1,200 words sampled across each member's corpus, then averaged per member. The display-only status and the +0.064 behavioural-diagonal mean vs the .12 bar were not found in this file.
evidence.transfer: The paper compares fine-tuned encoder language models (the BERT family) on self-report labels, not zero-shot instruction-tuned LLM item readers. It bears on model size only indirectly, so it cannot confirm the Pink miss.

evidence.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
evidence.claim: The same GBDT and RFR models are run with and without personality features. Average MSE improvement: GBDT 14.29 percent (CH 20.91, SG&A 31.74, ROA 12.52), RFR 6.67 percent. GBDT gains from CNN-1 features 3.38, CNN-2 minus 1.80, BERT 8.62. Gains for all eight DVs are significant by Wilcoxon, GBDT at p below 0.01. Observations per DV range 405 to 519 (Table 10). A chronological split is reported in Online Appendix G.
evidence.system_side: fec/members/behavioral_dispositions.py header: a label-free validation indicted the lexical Big Five for behavioural prediction (C reversed on participation, r_alerting -0.76), so dispositions are measured from behaviour. fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:58-64 defaults the basis to behavioral; the RECEPT_TRAITS environment variable reverts to lexical.
evidence.transfer: Borrow the design only: the same learner with and without a trait block, a held-out chronological split, and paired tests, applied to compare text traits against dispositions on a pre-registered responsiveness outcome. The lift magnitudes come from executives and firm accounting outcomes with reverse causality the authors leave unresolved, so they must not be quoted as evidence that text traits predict member behaviour.

evidence.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
evidence.claim: The authors restrict their evaluation to social posts, forum messages and essays, and say speech transcripts and written articles may warrant exploration. The downstream case applies a model fine-tuned on Facebook labels to executives' tweets, and the text reports no executive-level survey validation.
evidence.system_side: fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:65-73 defaults the N slot to affective (RECEPT_N environment variable). The cited fec/members/affective_n_validate.py:54-55 defines liwc_n, a lexical count-based N, and does not contain the rho .050 and .161 genre-transfer results.
evidence.transfer: Support is for caution only. The paper runs no transfer test of its own, so it neither confirms nor explains the system's genre-transfer result.

evidence.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
evidence.claim: Validity evidence is agreement with self-report surveys on non-elite authors. User-level Pearson correlations are at least 10 to 18 points above the best comparator and MSE at least 10 percent lower, reported in Online Appendix B and not in the body. No observer, expert or criterion validation is reported, and executive scores are used without survey validation.
evidence.system_side: Gold-panel validation runs through fec/members/b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py (insider and academic panels) and fec/members/b5_gold_criterion_probes.py. The pass pattern in the analyst's summary (E and A on both panels, O and N on one, C on insider only) was not verified against any results file.
evidence.transfer: The paper's standard is self-report agreement on non-elite authors. It is weaker than and different in kind from the system's observer-panel standard, so its figures cannot substitute for a gold-panel look.

evidence.title: Using Linguistic Cues for the Automatic Recognition of Personality in Conversation and Text
evidence.claim: SMOreg trained on EAR observer ratings (96 speakers, 10-fold CV) has relative absolute error above the mean baseline for all five traits: E 140.05, ES 162.05, A 173.97, C 131.75, O 213.20 percent (baseline 100). The authors say linear regression and SVMs perform poorly and suggest they need a bigger dataset.
evidence.system_side: fit_smoreg_rkh.py takes Ramey per-member trait averages as targets. big5_traits.py loads liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json as ACTIVE weights when the file exists, replacing the published-correlate weights.
evidence.transfer: Holds as a statement about the Mairesse observer model and Ramey fn 4. The paper never says what data the distributed observer model was fit on, so the claim that it was fit on all 96 speakers is an assumption. Ramey line 191 calls the training sample the essay sample, so Ramey is internally inconsistent on provenance.

evidence.title: Using Linguistic Cues for the Automatic Recognition of Personality in Conversation and Text
evidence.claim: On the essays corpus with self-reports, SMO binary accuracy is 54.9 to 62.1 percent (openness 62.1 vs 50.3 baseline). SMOreg relative error is E 100.65, ES 98.35, A 100.28, C 99.30 (none significant) and O 94.19 (significant). Best Pearson r is 0.33 for openness and 0.24 for emotional stability.
evidence.system_side: fit_smoreg_essays.py refits a LinearSVR on binary y/n labels (0/1 targets) and searches 12 settings on the same folds.
evidence.transfer: Paper figures verified. Table 12 SMO values are E 54.93, ES 57.35, A 55.78, C 55.29, O 62.11, so the 55 to 62 range is rounded. The grid search picks the best of 12 settings on the same folds, so its CV figure is optimistic, as stated. The paper's binary accuracies are not comparable to the system's refit since the features differ (Empath-augmented).

evidence.title: Using Linguistic Cues for the Automatic Recognition of Personality in Conversation and Text
evidence.claim: On EAR, observer-rated Naive Bayes beats baseline for E 73.00 vs 47.78, ES 73.89 vs 51.11 and C 67.67 vs 47.78. No self-report classifier or regressor significantly beats baseline. Mean inter-observer pair r is 0.54 for E, 0.29 for ES and 0.51 for C (18 observers, 31 to 33 pairs).
evidence.system_side: b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py evaluates predictions separately against the senate_insiders and academic_experts panels; the E and N pass results are system outputs, not checked here.
evidence.transfer: The EAR design is verified: observers rated audio only, without knowing the participants, in three groups, and the ratings were averaged (EAR description p.464-465). The Senate known-figure reputation point is outside the paper, and the paper never discusses Senate panels. Linking the ES observer agreement to the system's N gate is the verifier's inference.

evidence.title: Using Linguistic Cues for the Automatic Recognition of Personality in Conversation and Text
evidence.claim: In conversation only a high word count and a low mean pitch mark ES in both self and observer reports. Observed ES tracks swearing and anger words but self-assessed ES does not. Self-references and negative-emotion words mark neuroticism in essays, citing Pennebaker and King.
evidence.system_side: emit_affective_n.py keeps the LIWC i + negemo - posemo term only as a convergent anchor (r +.24), not as a component.
evidence.transfer: The paper compares essays and student conversation, not political genres, so the link to floor speech is an analogy. The genre-transfer rho values (.050, .161) are not checked here and are not in the paper.

evidence.title: Politics of Feelings: Emotional Expression and Legislative Effectiveness in the U.S. Congress
evidence.claim: Mixed models of speech-level emotion (Tables 5-6; n = 1,766,113 speeches; session and topic fixed effects): senators express less anger (-0.041, CI -0.043 to -0.039) and more pride (+0.009) and joy (+0.008); women express more fear (+0.004) and sadness (+0.006); majority members express less anger (-0.035); ideology score predicts more anger (+0.022). Mann-Kendall trends (Table 3, 26 Congresses): 15 of 16 party-by-emotion series increase significantly; Democratic joy does not (tau 0.243, FDR p 0.086).
evidence.system_side: affective_n is the mean of LLM affective facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility), residualized on E and then on a Republican dummy only; it is not residualized on chamber, gender or ideology. The LIWC-style anchor is a hand-written regex approximation (FPS, NEG, POS patterns), not the LIWC dictionary. The interview-to-floor transfer result (rho .050) was not located in this file.
evidence.transfer: Holds only weakly. Within one Congress majority status is nearly collinear with party, so the party residual may cover it. Chamber and gender are not covered and are a plausible structural confound. The paper's coefficients are mostly 0.001 to 0.04 in standardized units. The paper's facets are fear and sadness on floor text, not the interview facets used here.

evidence.title: Large language models know how the personality of public figures is perceived by the general public
evidence.claim: Perceived Big Five of public figures is predictable from the name embedding alone: cross-validated r = .78 (extraversion) to .88 (openness) after attenuation correction, raw .70-.80, N = 226 figures, 20-fold CV ridge on GPT-3 name embeddings; accuracy higher for more popular figures (r = .16 with log Wikipedia page views).
evidence.system_side: fec/members/big5_llm.py de-identifies name parts, titles, party words and 50 state names before item scoring (deidentify, lines 196-204). The module docstring (lines 11-14) cites Cao and Kosinski as the reason, but gives the venue as PNAS Nexus 2024 and r = .76-.87, which match neither the paper's venue nor its figures.
evidence.transfer: The paper uses GPT-3 name embeddings and lay ratings of globally famous figures, not a chat model reading congressional text. Transfer to the Pink reader is by analogy and untested.

evidence.title: Large language models know how the personality of public figures is perceived by the general public
evidence.claim: The paper uses name embeddings only. It does not test whether removing names from surrounding text removes the signal. It notes predictions reflect only the period in the training data, and that extension to people absent from training data is untested.
evidence.system_side: deidentify (big5_llm.py lines 196-204) blanks name parts longer than 2 characters, a fixed title list, party words and 50 state names, within 1,200-word chunks (CHUNK_WORDS = 1200 at line 51). Committee names, district cities and bill names are not removed. The --named probe (line 172, 30 members) is coded, but data/members holds only big5_llm_opus.json and big5_llm_sonnet.json plus caches, with no _named artifact. Name-part matching is case-insensitive, so common-word surnames also blank ordinary text.
evidence.transfer: Matters only where Pink scores feed a validity claim. The de-identification rationale is the code docstring's, not the paper's; the paper discusses a privacy threat from extracting traits from data (Discussion p.6), not text de-identification. The rel's Pink display-only status and the +.064 diagonal figure were not found in the brain concepts folder and remain unverified.

evidence.title: Large language models know how the personality of public figures is perceived by the general public
evidence.claim: Controlling for likability plus birth year and gender lowers accuracy from corrected r = .78-.88 to r = .53-.70 (raw .43-.61). The paper attributes the likability-trait links to the personality halo effect and reports that the least likable figures sit at undesirable extremes of several traits.
evidence.system_side: big5_ctcm.py (lines 8-9) puts an orthogonal PINK METHOD factor over the five Pink indicators to absorb judge halo. big5_ctcm2.py (lines 3-8) repeats this with the embedding Blue as third indicator. The ct_p2 function in big5_improvements_eval.py (around line 223) removes the first principal component as the general evaluative factor. The paper contains no method factor and no single-factor model; the consistency with the CT-CM design is the analyst's inference.
evidence.transfer: The paper's halo is in lay perceptions of famous people, with likability measured per figure. The rel says Melange has no per-member likability covariate; that was not checked here. The method factor is identified only by model structure, so the evidence bears on the halo's shape, not its size in congressional text.

evidence.title: Large language models know how the personality of public figures is perceived by the general public
evidence.claim: Perceptions of public figures track likability and demographics: birth year with extraversion, human r = .35 and model r = .44; women are perceived as more agreeable; an individual rater agrees with the aggregate at r = .56-.66.
evidence.system_side: The brain file (single-look-holdout-discipline-case-1-moneyball-gate2.md, line 35) states A-ES is about .44 population-real (RKH benchmark .443 House, .393 Senate) plus about .21 text-tone halo. That line does not mention gold panels, expert or insider ratings, k=1 insiders or rater independence. The code_ref big5_improvements_eval.py:10 is a --p1 docstring line and does not discuss gold panels. The RKH benchmark appears to be the Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh text measure, not a rater panel.
evidence.transfer: The paper's raters are lay Prolific workers rating world figures they recognise, not Hill insiders. The halo's size in Hill expert panels is untested by this paper. The gold-panel component is affected only if its raters use reputation and likability.

evidence.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress
evidence.claim: Broad communion correlates r = -0.36 with monthly Gallup approval (Model 3 beta +0.04, n.s.) while the prosocial helping facet correlates r = +0.55 (Model 3 beta +0.14, p < 0.05). Agency r = -0.16 and Model 3 beta -0.11 (p < 0.05). Window Jan 1996 to Nov 2014, N = 206 House months. Pooled over the whole chamber, not stratified.
evidence.system_side: The persona channel forms a z blend of two LLM cue shares from agency_communion_llm.py: persona z = 0.60 z(communion) - 0.40 z(agency). It is blended into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30 for members with at least 15 classified sentences (510 of the 526 rows in agency_communion.json meet this). The communion share uses the Empathy and Compassion codebook: STRONG cues name concrete disadvantaged people, while WEAK cues include empathic focus on communities and states. Group-intimacy or belonging talk has no dedicated cue.
evidence.transfer: The paper is about an aggregate chamber-month audience outcome (approval of Congress), not member-level susceptibility to lobbyists. The facet lesson transfers only as a construct-definition check: a pooled communion score can mix facets with opposite signs. Ecological inference from chamber months to individual members is not licensed.

evidence.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress
evidence.claim: Agency and communion indexes are built from coder-weighted LIWC category densities: five blind coders, ICC agency 0.82 and communion 0.90, averaged into category weights (weights independent, r = -0.03). A 127-word prosocial dictionary is scored alongside. Robustness to the coding is reported only in the Supplement.
evidence.system_side: The persona shares come from one instrument: Claude few-shot cue classification of self-referential floor and hearing sentences, cached per model. agency_communion_llm.py codes no second instrument for the same shares, so a dictionary path would have to be added as a second path.
evidence.transfer: A dictionary path would be a convergence check (DE-062 second path), not a validity test. The coder weights were set on chamber aggregates, so member-level densities on short self-referential samples would be noisy. The paper's ICCs describe agreement on category weights, not on member-level scores.

evidence.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress
evidence.claim: Chamber-level LIWC densities in House floor speech co-move with monthly approval. Exploratory stepwise standardized betas, UNSTRATIFIED: tentativeness +0.46, prepositions +0.41, humans +0.25, anxiety +0.24, positive emotion +0.24, numbers +0.15; second person -0.18, conjunctions -0.26 (8 of 63 categories kept, N = 206 months).
evidence.system_side: big5_traits.py standardizes per-1000-word category rates (posemo and tentat are among the CAT categories) within the corpus. The corpus pools each member's social posts with floor speech and interview text (CREC and INTERVIEW sources; CHRG excluded by default), not floor speech alone. BIG5_BEFORE and BIG5_AFTER are validation hooks that default to off, so no period slicing or de-trending applies by default.
evidence.transfer: Inference, not tested: if category rates drift by period at the chamber level, members whose speech is concentrated in different years could pick up period variance in their trait z. The paper shows co-movement, not the size of the drift. A per-year de-meaning test on Paul's corpus would check it.

evidence.title: The Bipartisan Path to Effective Lawmaking
evidence.claim: Offering cross-party cosponsorships predicts attracting them (Table 4; DV attracted share, IV offered share). House pooled Model 4.1 0.626 SE 0.039; House member FE Model 4.2 0.317 SE 0.036; Senate pooled Model 4.3 0.739 SE 0.045; Senate FE Model 4.4 0.547 SE 0.047; all p<0.001. Distance from median: House pooled -0.154, FE 0.005 (n.s.); Senate pooled -0.114, FE -0.096.
evidence.system_side: coop_v2_candidate.py composite = mean of z(c1) and z(c2). c1 is the bipartisan.json undirected cross-party share. c2 is the directional offered cross-party share from bills the member chose to join. c3 reciprocity is reported and never composited. receptivity_layer.py:183 records coop v2 as a near-duplicate of bpf (rho +0.888), a system-internal overlap, not paper evidence.
evidence.transfer: The paper is a member-level aggregate over 1973-2016, by chamber. Pooled and FE coefficients differ: the House roughly halves under FE, the Senate falls by about a quarter, so quote by chamber with strata. The paper shows offered-to-attracted reciprocity only, not that the composite tracks any effectiveness outcome.

evidence.title: No Longer Conforming to Stereotypes? Gender, Political Style, and Parliamentary Debate in the UK
evidence.claim: Communal styles (human narrative, affect, positive emotion) were higher among female MPs early in the period. Positive emotion and affect show no consistent significant gender gap by the latest years; the human narrative gap narrows gradually but is not stated to reach zero. For six of eight styles gender explains less between-MP style variation at the end of the period than at the start. For the converging styles the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls 29 to 60 percent comparing pre-2007 with post-2007; the converging styles are not named individually. Window: UK Commons May 1997 to March 2019. Denominator: MP-by-session variation (R2-style metric).
evidence.system_side: persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) - .40 z(agency) from LLM cue shares (agency_communion_llm.py), blended at PERSONA_W 0.30 for members with 15 or more classified sentences (receptivity_layer.py). No gender term in the persona code. Comments record cooperation_v2 gender -.021 and reactivity as gender-clean. The claimed party signature (communion D .099 vs R .049) was not found in fec/members or the audit files searched.
evidence.transfer: The paper gap is on UK floor speech using embedding-expanded dictionaries; the system uses Birkenmaier-Lechner LLM cue shares on US congressional sentences, a different instrument. Transfer holds only if US cue shares show a gender gap. Check: persona_susc_z against the legislators.csv gender column, partialled on party. Stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: No Longer Conforming to Stereotypes? Gender, Political Style, and Parliamentary Debate in the UK
evidence.claim: Negative emotion runs against the stereotype: women use more of it than men for much of 1997-2019. Gender explains about 2 percent of MP-level variation in negative emotion in 1997-2007 and about 9 percent after 2007. For negative emotion the divergence is almost entirely differential replacement of MPs, with a near-zero within-MP gender difference (supplement Fig S8). The main text says neither replacement nor within-MP change alone explains the convergence across styles. Window: UK Commons 1997-2019.
evidence.system_side: affective_n is the sum of LLM affective facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility), residualized on E then on party and z-scored (emit_affective_n.py). The LIWC composite is kept only as a convergent anchor (r +.24 per code comment). The file has no gender term, so there is no gender residualization or gender audit. Input source (interview text) was not traced further.
evidence.transfer: Applies only if US members negative-affect expression differs by gender in the interview genre. The paper measures negative emotion as a dictionary score on UK floor speech, not the LLM facets, so this is a different operationalisation. Any chamber-composition effect needs a stated window. The interview-genre transfer figures cited by the analyst were not rechecked.

evidence.title: No Longer Conforming to Stereotypes? Gender, Political Style, and Parliamentary Debate in the UK
evidence.claim: Seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe word embeddings correlate with human coder judgements at 0.61 to 0.85 per style across the comparison and intensity tasks. Standard dictionaries do worse, e.g. positive emotion 0.38 and 0.34 against 0.70 and 0.71 for the embedding measure. Each coder completed about 70 comparisons per style on average. Six of eight styles use the embedding expansion, and the embedding measure beats standard dictionaries for every style except fact (bootstrap test).
evidence.system_side: Closed-vocabulary posemo, negemo, anx and anger rates use published-exemplar word lists of about 20 to 32 words each (big5_traits.py), replaced by licensed LIWC .dic files if dropped into fec/liwc. Rates are z-scored and enter trait fits through weights. The paper validation covers UK debate sentences, not these lists.
evidence.transfer: The paper validation is on UK House of Commons sentences with two coders. Using its embedding expansion on congressional text needs a fresh human-coded sample. Any change to trait inputs falls under change control and single-look discipline. This is not a finding that the current lists are wrong.

evidence.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
evidence.claim: Sec 3.3 and Figs 3-4: sentence-by-sentence then averaged GPT-4o scores track expert coding on manifestos at r=0.98 (economic) and 0.94 (social). GPT-4 gives 0.98 and 0.92. Single whole-manifesto prompts (App G.2, Figs A12-A13) give economic r 0.96 to 0.98, similar to sentence scoring, and social r 0.83 to 0.92 with weaker within-party fit. Sec 4 says the paper has no clear recommendation on chunk versus single prompt. Sentences with NA are dropped from the average, not coded 0.
evidence.system_side: big5_llm.py de-identifies author name, state, party and title before scoring, codes cannot-tell as 0 among -1/0/+1 item responses, uses about 1,200-word chunks sampled across each corpus, and averages upward. The +0.064 versus 0.12 gate and the display-only status are not in this file.
evidence.transfer: The paper's units are single sentences from party manifestos and speeches, not chunks of member speech, and it drops NA rather than coding it 0. The paper does not discuss de-identification or name priors, so the claim that its senator r=0.97 reflects name priors is the analyst's speculation. The paper does not say whether names were removed from senators' tweets. The traits differ, so it cannot rescue the failed behavioural gate.

evidence.title: Playing to the Gallery: Emotive Rhetoric in Parliaments
evidence.claim: Within the same MP (MP fixed effects), PMQ speeches score 1.562 to 1.663 points higher on the emotive-minus-neutral scale than other debates (Table 3 Models 3-5; speech-level SD 8.95; UK 2001-2019, 958,925 speeches). The Queen's Speech opening day is 2.064 in Model 5. The authors read this as a venue pattern and say it is not causally identified.
evidence.system_side: The default corpus pools social posts, CREC floor speech and INTERVIEW turns per member into one text list (CHRG excluded by default). Per-member category rates are per-1000-word. Genre is only a validation hook (BIG5_SOURCES), not a covariate, so members with different venue mixes can differ in affect rates for venue reasons.
evidence.transfer: Applies only if US floor speech, interviews and social posts differ in audience exposure the way PMQs differs from ordinary Commons debate. The paper covers UK and Irish lower houses with a valence-agnostic ANEW-based score, not LIWC posemo/negemo. The speech-level shift is about 0.18 SD. Observational, not causal.

evidence.title: Playing to the Gallery: Emotive Rhetoric in Parliaments
evidence.claim: The authors argue, without causal identification, that legislators raise emotive rhetoric when addressing voters: PMQ speeches are higher within the same MP (about +1.6, Table 3) and Irish Leaders' Questions higher by +2.5 to +4.6 (Table 5, N=945,734). The paper does not test whether speakers keep their rank order in affect across venues.
evidence.system_side: affective_n is built from INTERVIEW turns only (source filter in emit_affective_n.py), and the recorded transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text failed. The paper gives a plausible venue mechanism for that failure. The rho values cited in the item (.050, .161) were not found in the cited code or in fec/members text files checked in this pass.
evidence.transfer: Explains, does not prove, the transfer failure. The paper tests average venue shifts, not member rank-order preservation, which is what rho measures. Does not license re-scoring floor text.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Can Infer Psychological Dispositions of Social Media Users
evidence.claim: Zero-shot holistic 1-5 Big Five ratings by GPT-4 from the last 200 Facebook updates (20-message chunks, chunk means, three queries averaged) correlate with IPIP-100 self-report at mean r .31 for GPT-4 and .27 for GPT-3.5 (n = 1,000 users; pooled average .29; per-trait range .22-.33 across both models). Supervised in-domain models reach about .37 (Park et al., as cited in Sec 4.1).
evidence.system_side: big5_llm.py is an item-level reader: 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items (4 per trait), 3-point responses (-1/0/+1), de-identified author text, default model Claude Sonnet (Opus and Haiku optional), chunks of 1,200 words with up to 6 chunks per genre, chunk scores averaged and then z-scored within the scored pool. The vault topic note records a diagonal mean over A, E and O of +0.064 for the Opus run (ES sign-flipped), below the 0.12 bar.
evidence.transfer: Holds only for informal first-person posts by ordinary young users scored against self-report. Member floor speech and interviews differ in genre and have no self-report criterion. The paper reports one accuracy level for one holistic prompt on one sample. It does not state a ceiling, so the figure is a reference point, not a bound. The item-level, de-identified design differs from the paper's holistic prompt.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Can Infer Psychological Dispositions of Social Media Users
evidence.claim: Each inference was queried three times and averaged. Between-round correlations ranged from .73 (GPT-4, Openness) to .96 (GPT-3.5, Agreeableness), so single-call noise is not negligible.
evidence.system_side: The primary score uses rep 0, a single call per chunk. The --rep flag reruns the same chunks with fresh calls to compute ICC across reps; those reps are not averaged into the published score.
evidence.transfer: Applies if the item-level Claude ratings show between-rep variance like the paper's. The paper is a holistic prompt on GPT models, so the size does not transfer directly. Any change to published scores would be new agent analysis, UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: Large Language Models Can Infer Psychological Dispositions of Social Media Users
evidence.claim: In 68 users rated by Facebook friends on a 10-item IPIP, LLM-observer agreement averaged r .269 (GPT-3.5) and .276 (GPT-4), against .304 for self-report-observer agreement. For Conscientiousness, LLM-observer agreement exceeded the agreement of either the LLM or observers with self-report. The analysis is described as preliminary.
evidence.system_side: Big Five validity is anchored to observer panels: the Personality on the Hill appendix, given in the vault gold-set note as 129 Senate insiders and 125 academics. The research note on that appendix counts about 126 academic rows from the text. The gold-set note names observer panels as the only anchor.
evidence.transfer: If LLM readings track the same outward impressions that observers form, convergence with expert or insider panels may index shared reputation or presentation rather than the underlying trait. The evidence is preliminary (n = 68) and rests on friends rating peers, not experts rating senators.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Can Infer Psychological Dispositions of Social Media Users
evidence.claim: Inferred Neuroticism correlates with self-report at r .29 for GPT-4 and .26 for GPT-3.5 (n = 1,000). Both models overestimate N. Absolute N residuals are larger for men (t = -4.55 GPT-3.5; t = -2.39, p = .017 GPT-4), while within-gender correlations do not differ significantly, so the bias is in level, not rank order.
evidence.system_side: RECEPT_N defaults to affective. The N slot takes an LLM affective-facet measure (the sum of Haiku pessimism, anxiety, depression and volatility labels), E-residualized and party-controlled, and enters the trait susceptibility term at weight .30. Missing values are set to a neutral 0.
evidence.transfer: The paper's pattern suggests within-pool z removes common level bias, but a demographic level offset would pass into a mixed-gender roster. Relevant only if the Haiku facet prompts on interview text share GPT's level bias by gender. The paper's N is an IPIP trait score on social media posts; the system input is a facet sum on interview text.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Can Infer Psychological Dispositions of Social Media Users
evidence.claim: Correlations rise with message volume from one 20-message chunk to ten chunks, but a substantial share of variance is captured with 20 messages and most correlations are close to their maximum well before 200 messages. Conscientiousness levels off earliest (Sec 3.1, Fig 2).
evidence.system_side: P6 gated shrinkage pulls members with fewer than 8 chunks toward 0. Interview chunks get double weight (C_INT_W 2.0) for Conscientiousness only.
evidence.transfer: The saturation volume comes from personal, cue-dense posts. Political text carries few personality cues, so saturation probably needs far more text. The paper's curve should not be used to relax the n_chunks gate. 20 messages at 17.10 words each is about 342 words, one 1,200-word chunk is much larger.

evidence.title: Measuring Emotion in Parliamentary Debates with Automated Textual Analysis
evidence.claim: Labor disputes Granger-cause opposition polarity (chi2 8.048, p=0.005) but not government polarity (chi2 0.092, p=0.761), from annual pairwise augmented VAR tests on the Westminster series (Table 4 bottom). The text says the labor-dispute impulse response appears greater for opposition (S5 Fig, not extracted). The authors frame these as associations and argue the mechanism from theory, not from an exogenous shock.
evidence.system_side: affective_n is a z-score of E-residualized LLM facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility) from interview text, then residualized on a Republican dummy. A LIWC-style count (fps + negemo - posemo) is computed only as the convergent-validity anchor. Majority status and interview date or period are not controlled.
evidence.transfer: The paper covers one Westminster chamber, aggregated over time, not individual-level US data. The extracted text does not state the frequency of the Table 4 tests, and S5 also has quarterly models. Within one Congress, party and majority status coincide, so the party control absorbs role; the chamber-flip window in the rel is the analyst's premise, not from this paper, and is untested here. Treat it as a possible confound only.
